opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think of it the way I think of most things, as a machine, and it works for a person much the way it works for a country. Debt is just a way of buying something today with money you're promising to pay back tomorrow. So when you borrow, you're able to spend more than you earn for a while, and it feels good, but you've also created a future obligation. You'll have to spend less than you earn when it comes time to pay it back. That's the cycle.

Now, over a lifetime, there's a natural arc to it. When you're young, you're earning relatively little, so it makes sense to borrow, to invest in your education or buy a home. In your middle years, you're earning the most, so you pay down that debt and you save. Then, when you retire, you stop earning and you live off those savings. If you've managed it well, that's a healthy pattern, because the debt went toward things that increased your ability to produce income or built up your assets.

The key thing is the difference between debt that's productive and debt that isn't. If you borrow and it makes you more productive, so that it pays for itself, that's good debt. If you borrow simply to consume, you've got the obligation but nothing to service it with. That's when the trouble starts, because your debt service, the interest and principal you have to pay, starts to squeeze out your other spending. Think of it like plaque building up in the arteries. It gradually constricts the circulatory system of your finances, and you have less and less room to spend on the things you need or want.

So my advice is simple: think of your income, your expenses and your savings the way a business thinks about its income statement and balance sheet. Make sure your debt is growing no faster than your income, and build up savings, because savings give you staying power and options. Being a creditor rather than a debtor is what gives you freedom. And the same logic that applies to you applies to a government, which is what people often miss. It's the same machine, just at a much larger scale.

r001.rationale: The response discusses paying down debt and building savings, but does not state that wiping out existing debt restores capacity to accumulate new debt.

r002.rationale: It explains that debt service—interest and principal payments—eventually squeezes out other spending and constricts financial capacity.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think of it the way I think of almost everything, which is as a machine. Debt is a cycle, and the cycle happens for very simple, almost mechanical reasons. When you borrow, you get to spend more than you earn today. That feels great. But what you've really done is you've created an obligation to spend less than you earn at some point in the future, because you have to pay it back. So borrowing is just pulling spending forward from the future to the present. And when a lot of people do that at the same time, you get a boom, and when they all have to pay it back, you get the squeeze.

Over a lifetime, what you see is that there's a short-term version of this and a long-term version. The short-term cycle, the one most people are familiar with, lasts maybe five to eight years. Credit gets easy, people borrow, spending and asset prices go up, inflation picks up, the central bank tightens, there's a recession, debts get cleaned up a bit, and then it starts again. You go through a number of those in your life, and you learn to recognize them.

But what's much harder to see is that each of those cycles tends to end with a little more debt than it started with, because the people in charge, quite understandably, would rather stimulate than let people go through pain. So the debt ratchets up, cycle after cycle, over decades. That's the long-term debt cycle, and it typically plays out over something like seventy five to a hundred years, which is roughly a lifetime. That's exactly why it's so dangerous. Nobody alive has really experienced the end of the last one. The people who went through the 1930s are mostly gone. So each generation thinks the conditions they grew up in are normal, when actually they're just one stage of a much bigger arc.

I learned this the hard way. In 1982 I was very confident that we were going into a depression because of the debt problems in Latin America, and I was publicly wrong. I lost almost everything, I had to let everyone go, I borrowed four thousand dollars from my dad to pay the bills. And what that taught me was that I didn't understand the mechanics well enough, that I needed to study every case in history, not just the ones I'd lived through. So I went back and studied all the big debt crises, going back hundreds of years, and you see the same pattern repeat over and over. The names change, the technology changes, the human nature doesn't.

So the way I'd put it to anyone listening is, you have to understand where you are in the cycle, and you have to understand that the thing you've never seen in your lifetime is still entirely possible, because it's happened many times before.

r001.rationale: The response says debts are “cleaned up a bit” before the cycle starts again, but does not state that wiping out existing debt restores capacity to accumulate new debt.

r002.rationale: It explains that borrowing creates an obligation to spend less later to repay, and that repayment by many borrowers produces a squeeze.

astra-6.text:
I think the simplest way to understand debt is that borrowing allows you to spend more than you earn today, but it requires you to spend less than you otherwise could in the future. You’re bringing future spending into the present.

That isn’t necessarily a bad thing. The question is: what are you doing with the money? If you borrow to acquire something that increases your income enough to service the debt, that can improve your circumstances. But if you borrow simply to support spending that your income can’t sustain, you’re creating a problem for your future self.

And it builds gradually. You take on a payment, then another payment. When income is rising and credit is readily available, those commitments can feel manageable. But the debt payments remain even if your income falls.

So you have to look at the whole picture over time: your income, your spending, your assets, and what you owe. The limit isn’t just how much someone will lend you. It’s how much you can repay, including when things don’t go as well as you expect.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that wiping out existing debt restores the ability to accumulate new debt.

r002.rationale: It explains that debt payments remain even if income falls and that borrowing requires less spending later, describing debt service as a constraint over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the simplest way to understand debt is that borrowing lets you spend more than you earn today, but it means you’ll have to spend less than you earn in the future. You’re borrowing spending power from your future self.

Early in life, you might borrow to buy a home or get an education. And that can make sense if the benefit you get allows you to comfortably service that debt. The important thing isn’t simply how much debt you have; it’s how the payments compare with your income.

But your spending is somebody else’s income. So when people borrow and spend more, incomes rise, people appear more creditworthy, and lenders lend more. That reinforces itself. Then, eventually, debt payments grow faster than incomes, and spending has to slow. That’s when the process reverses.

So whether you’re looking at an individual over a lifetime or an economy, the basic question is: Is the borrowing creating the income that will allow you to pay it back?

r001.rationale: The response does not say that wiping out existing debt restores capacity to borrow more.

r002.rationale: It explains that debt payments eventually grow faster than incomes, forcing spending to slow.
